chunks: First: Al-Bazzafi, from Ahmad ibn Idris, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding a man who died leaving a female slave and two male slaves, so a brother of his inherited them, and he freed the two males, and the female gave birth to a boy. He said: They testified after their manumission that their master had made them witnesses that he used to have intercourse with the female, and that the pregnancy was from him. He said: Their testimony is valid, and they are returned as slaves as they were.

As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ibn Faddal, from Dawud ibn Ziyad, from Dawud ibn Farqad, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who was traveling with a female slave and two male slaves, and he said to them: 'You are free for the sake of Allah, and testify that what is in the belly of this female is from me.' She gave birth to a boy. When they returned to the heirs, they denied this and re-enslaved them. Then the two boys were freed after that, and they testified after their manumission that their first master had made them witnesses that what was in the belly of his female was from him. He said: Their testimony is valid for the boy, and the boy does not re-enslave them, because they have established his lineage, so it does not contradict the first report for two reasons: First, that the first report did not state that he had freed them, so for that reason it was permissible to re-enslave them according to what it contained. The second reason is that this can be understood as recommended, because it is recommended for the boy that they be freed, and that he not re-enslave them, inasmuch as they established his lineage according to what the report contained, even if it was not obligatory.
ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling on the testimony of freed slaves regarding their manumission and lineage in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi presents these narrations to elucidate the nuances of *istidlal* (using testimony to establish rights) in the context of *kitman al-nasab* (concealing lineage) and manumission. The first case establishes that testimony is valid even if the witnesses were not previously freed, while the second case distinguishes between obligatory and recommended manumission, showing how established lineage prevents re-enslavement. This highlights the Shia juristic principle that factual establishment of lineage (*ithbat al-nasab*) holds precedence over the potential right of heirs to reclaim slaves.
